notes.meaning: Jesus commands John to write to the messenger or leader of the church in Ephesus. Jesus describes Himself as the One who holds the leaders securely in His right hand and walks among the golden lampstands, which represent the churches. This shows that He is present with His people, protects them, and watches over everything they do.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators often understand the angel to be the local bishop, seeing these letters as evidence that single bishops had spiritual authority over early city churches.

notes.meaning: Jesus tells the church that He sees their hard work and steady endurance. They refused to tolerate wicked people in their midst, and they carefully examined traveling teachers who falsely claimed to be apostles, or special messengers sent by God. By testing what these teachers taught against the truth, the believers exposed them as liars.

The believers in Ephesus continued to stand firm under hardship without giving up. They suffered many difficult trials because of their loyalty to the name of Jesus. Even when the work was exhausting, they did not quit their devotion to Him.

Even though they worked hard and defended the truth, Jesus brings a serious correction against them. They had abandoned their first love, letting the warm, tender affection they once had for Christ and for one another grow cold. Good deeds and correct doctrine cannot replace heartfelt love for the Lord.

Jesus urges the church to remember how high they once stood and how far they have fallen. He calls them to repent, which means to change their minds and turn back to doing the loving deeds they practiced at the beginning. If they refuse to repent, Christ warns that He will remove their lampstand, ending their status as a true church.

Jesus praises the Ephesians for hating the wicked practices of a group known as the Nicolaitans. These people encouraged Christians to compromise with pagan society by excusing sexual sin and idol banquets under the banner of freedom. Jesus hates these corrupt actions because they harm people and dishonor God.

differ.view: Some evangelicals understand the Nicolaitans not as a licentious sect, but as an early movement that tried to set up a priestly ruling class over the common people in the church.

notes.meaning: Anyone with ears to hear is urged to listen closely to what the Holy Spirit is saying to all the churches. To the believer who overcomes temptation and remains loyal, Jesus promises the right to eat from the tree of life in God's heavenly paradise. This restores the gift of eternal life that was lost in the Garden of Eden.

differ.view: Many evangelicals believe that every true Christian is an overcomer through saving faith in Christ and will receive these heavenly promises.
Some evangelicals teach that overcomers are faithful believers who endure obediently to the end, earning special heavenly rewards beyond the gift of salvation itself.

notes.meaning: John is directed to write to the leader of the church in Smyrna, a city facing fierce persecution. Jesus introduces Himself as the First and the Last, the eternal God who experienced death on the cross and rose to life again. Because Jesus conquered the grave, His followers do not need to fear physical death.

Jesus knew all the painful trouble and outward poverty the Christians in Smyrna endured, likely from having their property stolen during persecution. Yet in God's sight they were spiritually rich with faith and heavenly treasures. Jesus also saw the slander hurled at them by people who claimed to be God's covenant people by blood, but acted as a gathering of Satan by opposing the gospel.

Jesus tells His people not to be afraid of the suffering that is about to come upon them. The devil was going to instigate local leaders to put some believers into prison to test their faith, but the tribulation would last for only a limited time, described as ten days. Christ promises that if they remain faithful even to the point of dying, He will hand them the crown of eternal life.

Every listener is called to pay attention to what the Holy Spirit speaks to the churches. The believer who overcomes through faith will never be harmed by the second death, which is final, eternal punishment away from God. Earthly enemies might kill the body, but they can never rob a Christian of everlasting life.

The letter to the church in Pergamum comes from the One who holds the sharp, two-edged sword. This sword represents the powerful word of God that cuts deep into human hearts and carries out divine judgment. Pergamum needed to hear from the supreme Judge because error was invading their fellowship.

Jesus recognized that this church lived in a city filled with rampant pagan worship and official hostility, which He calls the throne of Satan. In spite of severe pressure, the congregation stayed loyal to Christ and did not deny their faith in Him. They remained steadfast even when Antipas, a faithful witness for Jesus, was martyred in their city.

Jesus rebukes the church because some members accepted the teaching of Balaam. Long ago, the prophet Balaam showed King Balak how to lure the Israelites into sin through idol feasts and sexual immorality. In a similar way, false teachers in Pergamum were enticing Christians to compromise with pagan culture and join in immoral feasts.

The church also had people who followed the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Like Balaam, this group encouraged Christians to think that participating in pagan vice and immorality did not matter. While Ephesus had rejected these false teachers, Pergamum had failed to remove them from church fellowship.

Jesus commands the entire church to repent of their tolerance of these false teachers. If they refuse to turn away from this sin, Christ warns that He will come swiftly in judgment. He will wage war against the unrepentant deceivers using the sword of His spoken word.

All who hear are urged to listen to the Spirit's voice to the churches. To those who overcome worldly compromise, Jesus promises hidden manna, which is spiritual food and deep fellowship with Himself. He also promises a white stone marked with a new name, picturing personal pardon, warm welcome, and an intimate relationship with God that only the receiver understands.

John is instructed to write to the leader of the church in Thyatira on behalf of the Son of God. Jesus is described as having eyes like blazing fire, meaning He sees and knows every hidden secret, and feet like polished bronze, showing His holy strength to bring righteous judgment. His piercing vision sees both the good and the bad within the church.

Jesus warmly praises the believers in Thyatira for their love, faith, humble service, and patient endurance. Unlike the Ephesians, who had cooled off, the Christians in Thyatira were making steady progress. Their recent works were even greater and more fruitful than the deeds they performed at the start.

Despite their growing love, Jesus rebukes the church for tolerating a wicked woman whom He calls Jezebel. Claiming to be a prophetess who spoke for God, she seduced church members into sexual immorality and pagan feasts. The church was guilty because it allowed her to teach false freedom and lead believers into open sin.

Jesus explains that He gave this false teacher time to turn away from her sexual immorality and idolatry. God showed great patience toward her, but she stubbornly refused to repent. When sinners treat God's patience with contempt, judgment eventually follows.

Jesus warns that the bed of her sinful pleasure will become a bed of intense sickness and agony. Those who joined her in moral and spiritual unfaithfulness will also face severe suffering. The only way to escape this coming calamity is to repent immediately and turn away from her evil deeds.

Jesus declares that her devoted followers, described as her children, will be struck down by death. This severe judgment will show all the congregations that Christ examines the innermost thoughts, desires, and motives of every person. He will reward or punish each individual according to what they have really done.

Jesus addresses the faithful believers in Thyatira who refused to follow Jezebel's corrupted teaching. The false teachers claimed to offer deep spiritual secrets, but Jesus identified them as the deep schemes of Satan. Because these Christians remained pure, Christ promises not to place any other burden or new demands upon them.

Jesus tells the faithful believers to hold tightly to the truth, love, and purity they already possess. They are not to let anyone pry them away from their loyalty to the gospel. They must keep standing firm until Christ returns for them.

To the believer who overcomes temptation and keeps doing Christ's work until the end, Jesus promises authority over the nations. Faithful followers who seem weak and helpless in this world will one day share in the Messiah's kingdom. Christians who endure suffering now will be given royal responsibility in the future.

Drawing from Psalm 2, Jesus explains that His people will share in His unbreakable rule over the nations. Unbelieving and rebellious powers will be shattered completely, just like brittle clay pots smashed with an iron rod. Christ gives this authority to His faithful servants because He received it directly from His Father.

Jesus promises to give the victor the morning star. Because Christ Himself is the bright morning star, this promise means He will give Himself to His people in intimate communion. Believers will share in His heavenly brightness, glory, and life as a new day dawns.

The letter closes with the command for every person to listen carefully to what the Holy Spirit says to the churches. The warnings and promises given to Thyatira are meant for congregations throughout all generations. Everyone who has an ear to hear is called to take these truths to heart and follow the Lord with complete loyalty.
